doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Doubts, loving the subject, and teaching
summary: Crohn says he does his best work only on music he loves, discusses technical chops and why he is wary of film-school lecturing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Did you ever have moments where you are saying why am I doing this?

Oh yeah, of course. Of course. If I knew how to do anything else I’d probably be doing something else. I mean raising money, I’m getting older and running on location and doing this and producing this and worrying and this and that. But no, Warren talks about feeling blessed. I don’t think I’ve had the sort of like blessed life Warren had, where he started listening to music under the piano hearing Rubenstein playing. But I feel blessed that I’ve been able to — every film that I’ve done that’s been any good, that’s been seen © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

on television, has been about music. And there is something about — I don’t think I’m a great filmmaker at all. I mean there are people with way better technical chops than me. But if I love it, it seems to come out better. If I don’t love it, it doesn’t come out good at all. So I’m not good at doing commercials or doing industrial films, because if I don’t love it, there are twenty people that do it better than me — a hundred and twenty people — twelve hundred people.
What are technical chops in filmmaking?

Oh I don’t know, lighting and sound, and you know, image and effects. I don’t know. There’s a lot of stuff you have to learn, and I never learned it in film school so I’m always learning it as I go along. But that’s the way I learn. But I love learning like that.
Don’t you feel you could at least be a guest at a film school?

Just like you said that you — well you know you’ve had me out, I’ve guest lectured at film — I don’t know. They tend to go, I don’t know, I tend to put myself down so I don’t know. But I’m older, as you went through, you try for a teaching job and you may be too old for the teaching job, and you don’t have advanced degrees and I don’t have film school degrees. I’ve had certain experiences that I think can be valuable to impart — to pass on. I think I’m probably more valuable for some filmmaker to just call me up and ask me questions about stuff, because I don’t know if I lectured it at a film school whether it would be of interest to everybody. I believe education is where someone seeks out the person with knowledge, not where the person with knowledge comes and tells you what they think you need to learn. But sure, anybody that’s older has been through a lot of stuff and has something to impart. That’s the tradition of the elders in tribal communities. Instead of us getting older and being marginalized as we grow older, there’s a culture where there the elders are important. They may not be able to do everything they did when they were young, but they have accumulated wisdom to pass on.
